pages.title: 1. First queries
pages.body:
## Installing the CLI

[DuckDB] is a library: it runs inside the process that uses it, like SQLite. The [DuckDB CLI] is one such process, a single executable with no dependencies. It's the quickest way to start, and the one this course uses until lesson 5.

Open a new terminal afterwards so `duckdb` is on the `PATH`. The [CI of this course] downloads `duckdb_cli-windows-amd64.zip` from the [GitHub releases] instead, to pin the version: the executable only needs to be unzipped.

The script installs the binary in `~/.duckdb/cli//`, points `~/.duckdb/cli/latest` to it, and prints the line to add to your shell profile:

If `~/.local/bin` exists, it also creates a `duckdb` link there. On a GitHub runner: `Successfully installed DuckDB 1.5.5 to /home/runner/.duckdb/cli/1.5.5/duckdb`. Set `DUCKDB_VERSION=1.5.5` before `sh` to pin the version.

Or the same script as on Linux, which the CI of this course uses on `macos-latest`:

## The data

Clone this site's repository and go to the course folder, where the relative paths of every query in this course work:

`data/runs.json` is one JSON array of 125 objects, one per GitHub Actions run of this repository:

## A query on a file

Start the CLI with `duckdb`: it answers with its version and `Enter ".help" for usage hints.`, and an in-memory database. Then, without creating anything:

A file name in quotes is a table. DuckDB saw the `.json` extension, read the file, and inferred a type for each field: `bigint` for the numbers, `timestamp` for the ISO 8601 strings, `varchar` for the rest. In SQL Server, the closest thing is [`OPENROWSET(BULK …)`] with `OPENJSON` and an explicit `WITH` clause listing the columns and their types.

`DESCRIBE FROM 'data/runs.json'` is also a first taste of DuckDB's [friendly SQL]: `FROM` can come first, and a query with only `FROM` means `SELECT *`.

The first query of [`sql/01-first-queries.sql`]: which workflows run most, and how often they fail.

From [`sql/01-first-queries.sql`, lines 2-6]:

Two extensions to the SQL you know:

- [`GROUP BY ALL`] groups by every column of the `SELECT` that isn't an aggregate. No more copying the column list into `GROUP BY`.
- [`FILTER`] restricts one aggregate. The SQL Server way is `sum(CASE WHEN conclusion = 'failure' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`. `FILTER` is standard SQL, and PostgreSQL has it too.

`LIMIT` is `TOP` at the end of the query. The output format is `duckbox`, the CLI's default: column types under the names, and numbers aligned right.

## Reading the errors

A PostgreSQL habit, `snake_case` column names:

A **Binder Error** means the SQL parsed, but a name doesn't resolve. DuckDB suggests the closest names and points at the position. A table that doesn't exist yet gives a **Catalog Error**:

The suggestion is the closest name among the system views: a guess, not a hint that something is wrong with `duckdb_constraints`.

## First look at the data: `SUMMARIZE`

[`SUMMARIZE`] computes statistics for every column. It returns 12 columns, too wide for this page; since its result is a table like any other, a query can pick some:

What this says in a few seconds:

- 125 rows and no `NULL` anywhere: the snapshot only has completed runs (`status` has one value).
- The history covers less than a day: from 2026-09-13 15:53 to 2026-09-14 14:01.
- `attempt` goes up to 3: at least one run was re-run twice.
- `headBranch` has two values: `main`, and the branch of an experiment from the GitHub Actions course.
- **`approx_unique` is an estimate.** `databaseId`, the run id, is unique, yet 131 is more than the 125 rows. It uses [HyperLogLog], which trades exactness for constant memory. Exercise 2 finds the exact counts.
- `min` and `max` are `varchar` for every column, so they fit in one result column: `max` of `attempt` is the string `'3'`.

The timestamps in the file end with `Z` (UTC). DuckDB read them as `TIMESTAMP`, without a time zone: the values are the UTC times, and nothing in the type says so. Lesson 2 comes back to this.

## Keeping the rows: a table

Each query above read and parsed the JSON file again. To read it once, store the rows in a table ([`CREATE TABLE … AS`], the `SELECT INTO` of SQL Server) ([`sql/01-first-queries.sql`, lines 8-13]):

Manual runs (`workflow_dispatch`) failed 9 times out of 19; pushes, 7 out of 106. That matches how the GitHub Actions course was written: the exercise workflows, started by hand, were designed to fail.

The table lives in the in-memory database, and disappears when the CLI exits.

## Keeping the database: a file

The file name is the first argument of `duckdb`. The file is created if it doesn't exist:

Start it again with the same file, and the table is still there:

The database is named after the file. The `.duckdb` extension is a convention; DuckDB doesn't require it.

## Writing files: `COPY`

[`COPY … TO`] writes a table or a query result to a file, and picks the format from the extension:

The sizes, for the same 125 rows:

| File | Bytes |
|---|---|
| `data/runs.json` | 39,705 |
| `out/runs.csv` | 21,058 |
| `out/runs.parquet` | 8,553 |
| `out/ci.duckdb` | 536,576 |

[Parquet] is a compressed, columnar file format with types, and the one lesson 4 recommends for data you keep. The `.duckdb` file is the largest. A database file with nothing in it is 12,288 bytes of headers; data is stored in blocks of 262,144 bytes (`block_size` in `PRAGMA database_size`), and this one has two: 12,288 + 2 × 262,144 = 536,576. The format is made for millions of rows, not for 125.

`COPY` doesn't create folders. Without the `mkdir out` above:

The second half of that message is the Windows system error text.

## Two CLI settings

Dot commands configure the CLI itself. They are not SQL, and take no semicolon ([list]):

On 125 rows, every query takes about a millisecond: the timer only gets interesting in lesson 7. `.mode` changes the [output format]; `.mode line` shows one field per line, handy for wide rows:

## Scripts and CSV output: how this course is tested

The CLI also reads SQL from standard input, and `-csv` switches the output to CSV. [`check.sh`] runs every script of `sql/` that way and compares the result with the file of the same name in `sql/expected/`:

On a GitHub runner, for each of the three operating systems: `ok   01-first-queries`. [`-c`] runs a single command and exits, for one-liners in a terminal: `duckdb -c "FROM 'data/runs.json' LIMIT 3"`.

## Key takeaways

- DuckDB is a library that runs in your process; the CLI is one executable, and needs no server.
- A quoted file name is a table: DuckDB infers the format from the extension and the types from the content.
- `DESCRIBE` and `SUMMARIZE` are the first two commands to run on unknown data; `approx_unique` is an estimate.
- A table stays in memory unless the CLI was started with a database file; `COPY … TO` writes CSV, JSON or Parquet.
- Errors name their kind (`Binder`, `Catalog`, `IO`) and suggest the closest names.

## Exercises

The solutions are in [`sql/01-exercises.sql`], checked by CI like the lesson.

1. How many manual runs (`workflow_dispatch`) failed?

Solution

From [`sql/01-exercises.sql`, lines 3-5]:

The same number as the `workflow_dispatch` / `failure` row of the table above.

2. `SUMMARIZE` estimates 17 distinct workflow names and 59 distinct commits. What are the exact numbers?

Solution

From [`sql/01-exercises.sql`, lines 8-9]:

21 and 65: the estimate was low by about 10% on both, and high by 5% on the run ids. `count(DISTINCT …)` is exact but has to remember every value it has seen; `approx_count_distinct(…)` gives the same kind of estimate as `SUMMARIZE` in constant memory. On 125 rows, use the exact one.

3. The Binder Error above suggested `workflowName`. Would `workflowname`, all lowercase, work? And what would the column be called in the result?

Solution

From [`sql/01-exercises.sql`, lines 12-17]:

Yes. [Identifiers are case-insensitive] in DuckDB, "similarly to PostgreSQL", and also in double quotes, unlike PostgreSQL where `"workflowName"` and `workflowname` are two different names. The comparison is ASCII-only: `é` and `É` are different letters for it. DuckDB preserves the case of the name as it was defined, so the result column is `workflowName`, not the case typed in the query. `workflow_name` failed because the underscore makes it a different name, not because of the case.

## Sources

- [DuckDB CLI overview], [arguments], [dot commands] and [output formats]
- [Installation]
- [Loading JSON]
- [`DESCRIBE`] and [`SUMMARIZE`]
- [`COPY`]
- [Friendly SQL]
- [Keywords and identifiers]

pages.title: 2. Friendly SQL
pages.body:
Every query of this lesson is in [`sql/02-friendly-sql.sql`], run from `code/duckdb` like in [lesson 1]. The script starts by loading the runs into a table ([line 2]):

## Durations: timestamps and intervals

Subtracting two `TIMESTAMP` values gives an [`INTERVAL`], which `avg` and `max` accept ([lines 5-9]):

`HAVING runs >= 4` uses the alias of the `SELECT`: DuckDB allows it in `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, where SQL Server makes you repeat `count(*)`. The Java examples take the longest, as the [Java course] compiles and runs every lesson's code on three operating systems.

Two things the data doesn't tell you directly:

- `updatedAt` is the last time the run changed, and `startedAt` is the start of the **latest attempt**. The run of `GHA 09: debugging` that was re-run twice was created at 13:40:10 and started at 13:44:02: its duration only counts the third attempt. Lesson 3 uses the job timestamps instead.
- `sum` doesn't accept intervals, although `avg` does:

Convert to seconds first with `epoch(interval)` or `date_diff('second', startedAt, updatedAt)`, and back with `to_seconds(…)` if you want an interval again: `to_seconds(sum(epoch(updatedAt - startedAt)))` gives `00:51:10` for the 65 deployments of this site.

### Truncating: runs per hour

From [`sql/02-friendly-sql.sql`, lines 12-16]:

[`date_trunc`] is `DATETRUNC` in SQL Server 2022. A cast to `DATE` (`createdAt::DATE`) truncates to the day; `hour(…)`, `dayofweek(…)` and the other [date parts] extract a number.

## Time zones

GitHub writes `2026-09-13T15:53:16Z`: UTC. DuckDB read it as a [`TIMESTAMP`], a date and time with no zone, like `datetime2` in SQL Server. `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` (`TIMESTAMPTZ`) is an instant, like `DateTimeOffset` in C# or `Instant` in Java, **displayed in the session's time zone**. `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` says what zone a `TIMESTAMP` was in, and turns it into a `TIMESTAMPTZ` ([lines 19-23]):

Without the `SET`, the CLI uses the operating system's time zone. That's why the script sets it: GitHub runners are in UTC, and the expected output would not match anywhere else. Any output that shows a `TIMESTAMPTZ` depends on a setting, not only on the data. Time zone support comes from the [ICU extension], built into the CLI.

## Window functions

[Window functions] work as in SQL Server and PostgreSQL. The `WINDOW` clause names a window once, for several functions ([lines 26-33]):

The story of the Rust course's CI is readable in the gaps: a failure at 17:40, a second one 82 seconds later, fixed 53 seconds after that. Lesson 3 finds out which step failed.

## `QUALIFY`: filtering on a window function

Which workflows are red right now, that is, whose **last** run didn't succeed? In SQL Server, a window function can't appear in `WHERE`, so this takes a subquery or a CTE. [`QUALIFY`] is a `WHERE` evaluated after the window functions ([lines 36-40]):

The two conditions can't move to `WHERE`: `conclusion <> 'success'` in `WHERE` would remove the green runs **before** numbering, and every workflow with at least one failure would show up. All seven are exercises of the GitHub Actions course, red on purpose.

## `PIVOT`

[`PIVOT`] turns the values of a column into columns. Unlike [SQL Server's `PIVOT`], it doesn't need the list of values ([lines 43-47]):

- The columns are the values found in the data, so they change with the data: `startup_failure` exists in `runs`, but none of these four workflows had one, and the column isn't there. Code that reads a pivot by column name must expect that.
- Without `ORDER BY`, the order of the rows isn't defined. A first try of `PIVOT runs ON event USING count(*) GROUP BY conclusion` returned `success`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`, `failure`, in no useful order. The course scripts always end with `ORDER BY`, or their output couldn't be compared.

## Shortcuts for columns

From [`sql/02-friendly-sql.sql`, lines 50-54]:

- `headSha[1:7]` slices a string, both ends included, counting from 1: the short commit hash.
- [`COLUMNS('.*At')`] expands to every column whose name matches the regular expression, and `min(COLUMNS(…))` applies `min` to each: one aggregate written, three computed.
- `ORDER BY ALL` sorts by every column, left to right.
- `SELECT * EXCLUDE (headSha, status)` selects everything but some columns, and `SELECT * REPLACE (headSha[1:7] AS headSha)` changes one while keeping its place.

## Key takeaways

- Timestamps subtract into intervals; `avg` and `max` take intervals, `sum` doesn't: go through `epoch`.
- A `TIMESTAMP` has no zone; a `TIMESTAMPTZ` is displayed in the session's zone, so fix `TimeZone` in anything you compare.
- `QUALIFY` filters on window functions without a subquery.
- `PIVOT` finds its columns in the data; order the rows yourself.
- `GROUP BY ALL`, `ORDER BY ALL`, `COLUMNS`, `EXCLUDE` and aliases in `HAVING` remove repetition.

## Exercises

The solutions are in [`sql/02-exercises.sql`], checked by CI.

1. For each UTC day, how many runs, and what percentage didn't succeed, to one decimal?

Solution

From [`sql/02-exercises.sql`, lines 5-9]:

The second day is the one of the GitHub Actions course and its failing exercises. Note `100 * … / count(*)`: in DuckDB, `/` between two integers returns a `DOUBLE` (`7 / 2` is `3.5`), and `//` is the integer division. In SQL Server and in C#, the same expression would have truncated to `6` and `21`.

2. For each failed run, how long did its workflow stay red, that is, until the next successful run of the same workflow? List the failures that were never fixed first.

Solution

From [`sql/02-exercises.sql`, lines 12-18]:

- The window frame starts at `1 FOLLOWING`, the run after the failure; `FILTER` inside a window aggregate keeps only the successes. `min(createdAt)` is then the next green run.
- The filter on failures has to be in `QUALIFY`: in `WHERE`, it would remove the successes before the window looks for them, and every `red_for` would be `NULL`.
- `NULLS FIRST` puts the never-fixed failures on top; DuckDB sorts `NULL` last by default, in both directions.

3. Rewrite the `QUALIFY` query of this lesson, the workflows whose last run isn't green, without any window function.

Solution

From [`sql/02-exercises.sql`, lines 21-25]:

[`arg_max(value, key)`] returns `value` from the row where `key` is largest: the conclusion of the most recent run. The same seven workflows. `QUALIFY` is the general tool, since it can return whole rows or the top 3; `arg_max` is shorter when one value per group is enough.

## Sources

- [Interval functions], [timestamp functions] and [date parts]
- [Timestamp types] and [time zones]
- [Window functions], [`WINDOW`] and [`QUALIFY`]
- [`PIVOT`]
- [Star expressions: `COLUMNS`, `EXCLUDE`, `REPLACE`]
- [`ORDER BY`] and [aggregate functions]

pages.title: 3. Nested data
pages.body:
The runs of lessons 1 and 2 are flat: one value per field. Their jobs aren't. The queries are in [`sql/03-nested-data.sql`].

## The jobs file

`data/jobs.json` holds the 315 jobs of the runs, as returned by the GitHub REST API endpoint [List jobs for a workflow run], with a subset of the fields. For a run that was re-run, the API returns only the jobs of the latest attempt: 4 jobs for the `GHA 09: debugging` run attempted three times, where `?filter=all` returns 12. One job, shortened:

The JSON reader turned the arrays into [`LIST`] types, written `type[]`, and the objects into [`STRUCT`] types, with named and typed fields. `steps` is a list of structs. In C#, that's a `List` property on a `Job` record; in SQL Server, the JSON would stay a `nvarchar(max)` string, and every query would go through `OPENJSON` again.

## Reading into lists and structs

From [`sql/03-nested-data.sql`, lines 6-9]:

- **Lists start at 1**, as everywhere in SQL. `labels[0]` isn't an error, just `NULL`, and so is any index past the end: a C# or Java habit that fails silently.
- `steps[1].name` reads a field of a struct with a dot, like a property.
- `len` counts the elements of a list.

## `unnest`: one row per element

[`unnest`] turns a list into rows. Placed in the `FROM` clause after the table, it runs once per job, with access to that job's columns: the `CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(...)` of SQL Server, or `SelectMany` in LINQ.

From [`sql/03-nested-data.sql`, lines 12-15]:

`AS t(s)` names the table `t` and its single column `s`, a struct. This is the build job of the deployment of this site: 48 of its 58 seconds are in the `withastro/action` step. Step 4 is missing from the API response itself (`gh run view 34852867099 --json jobs` shows the same numbers); probably an internal step of that composite action, *to verify*.

## Aggregating nested data

The same pattern as flat data, once the list is unnested. The job timestamps give a better duration than the run fields of lesson 2, and one more: the time spent **waiting** for a runner, from `created_at` to `started_at`.

From [`sql/03-nested-data.sql`, lines 18-22]:

macOS runners take more than twice as long to start; Windows jobs run more than four times longer than Ubuntu jobs. Not a fair comparison, since most Ubuntu jobs are small ones like the site deployment; exercise 3 compares the same job on the three systems.

## Lambdas: working on a list without unnesting it

Which steps fail most? Each job keeps its failed steps in its own list; [`list_filter`] keeps the elements for which a [lambda] is true, before `unnest` turns what's left into rows ([lines 25-31]):

- Two of the three Rust failures of lesson 2 were formatting, `cargo fmt --check`, on each of the three operating systems; the third was a compile-fail doctest. `Run actions/setup-dotnet@v6` is the missing lock file of the GitHub Actions course, lesson 5.
- `lambda s: s.conclusion = 'failure'` is the C# lambda `s => s.Conclusion == "failure"`. `list_transform` is `Select`, `list_filter` is `Where`, `list_reduce` is `Aggregate`.
- `list(… ORDER BY …)` is an aggregate that builds a list: `STRING_AGG` without the string. Some values are quoted in the display (`'GHA 05: exercise checks'`) and others aren't (`Rust course examples`): the quotes belong to the display, not to the values.

The arrow syntax found in older examples still works in 1.5.5, with a warning:

## `ANTI JOIN`: rows without a match

125 runs in `runs.json`, but `count(DISTINCT run_id)` in `jobs` is 121. Which runs have no job? `NOT EXISTS` works, and so does DuckDB's [`ANTI JOIN`], which reads like what it does ([lines 34-37]):

All four are in the [GitHub Actions course journal]: the two pushes of a workflow file with invalid YAML, a manual run cancelled by a newer one before its job started, and the workflow calling another with an undeclared input. A run can fail without running anything. `SEMI JOIN` is the opposite: the rows that **have** a match, each once, like `EXISTS`.

## Building nested values

The other direction: grouping rows into a list of structs, with a struct literal `{'key': value}` ([lines 40-43]):

`to_json` turns any value into JSON text, for an API response or a file: `to_json({'job': 'commonjs', 'steps': [1, 2]})` gives `{"job":"commonjs","steps":[1,2]}`.

## Key takeaways

- JSON arrays become `LIST`, objects become `STRUCT`, with types; nested data stays queryable without parsing strings.
- Lists are indexed from 1, and an index out of range is `NULL`, not an error.
- `unnest` in the `FROM` clause turns a list into rows, like `CROSS APPLY` or `SelectMany`.
- `list_filter` and `list_transform` with `lambda x: …` work on a list in place.
- `ANTI JOIN` and `SEMI JOIN` say "without a match" and "with a match" directly.
- `list(…)` and `{'key': value}` build nested values back.

## Exercises

The solutions are in [`sql/03-exercises.sql`], checked by CI.

1. Some jobs have no step at all. Which ones, and what's in their `runner_name`?

Solution

From [`sql/03-exercises.sql`, lines 6-10]:

Three skipped jobs, which never got a runner: `NULL`. And a `deploy` job that failed with no step: the deployment from a branch other than `main`, rejected by the environment's branch policy in the GitHub Actions course. It got an **empty string** as runner name, not `NULL`. `WHERE runner_name IS NULL` would miss it: check both, or `coalesce(runner_name, '') = ''`, whenever the source is someone else's JSON.

2. `SELECT name, unnest(steps, recursive := true) FROM jobs` expands each step struct into columns. The job has a `name`, and so does each step. What are the columns called?

Solution

In the CLI display, two columns are both called `name`. Referencing them from an outer query shows the real names ([`sql/03-exercises.sql`, lines 13-16]):

The [deduplication rule] keeps the first `name` and renames the next one `name_1`. And `conclusion` is the **step's**: the job has no `conclusion` in this subquery, since only `name` was selected. When both sides have fields in common, alias them explicitly, as the lesson does with `j.name AS job, s.name AS step`.

3. `GHA 02: build and test` builds the same .NET and Java projects on three operating systems. What's the slowest step on each?

Solution

From [`sql/03-exercises.sql`, lines 19-25]:

On Windows and macOS, installing the .NET SDK costs more than any build or test. On Ubuntu, where it's faster, Maven's build and tests come first. `j.id, s.number` in the window's `ORDER BY` break ties: several steps can take the same whole number of seconds, and without a tie-breaker `row_number()` would pick one arbitrarily, possibly a different one on the next run.

## Sources

- [List] and [struct] types
- [`unnest`]
- [List functions] and [lambda functions]
- [`FROM` and joins, including `SEMI` and `ANTI`]
- [Loading JSON]
- [GitHub REST API: workflow jobs]

pages.title: 4. Files
pages.body:
So far, DuckDB read one JSON file at a time. This lesson writes and reads the other formats, and many files at once. The queries are in [`sql/04-files.sql`]. They write into `out/`, a folder that [`check.sh`] creates and Git ignores; create it by hand before running them yourself.

From [`sql/04-files.sql`, lines 3-4]:

## CSV: what the sniffer guesses

CSV has no types, no standard delimiter and no standard date format. To have a hard case, the script writes the runs the way a spreadsheet with French settings saves them: semicolons, day before month.

From [`sql/04-files.sql`, lines 7-8]:

When DuckDB reads a CSV file, the [CSV sniffer] reads a sample and guesses the dialect and the types. `sniff_csv` shows the guess without reading the file ([lines 11-12]):

The delimiter, the header and the integer column are right. `createdAt` is `VARCHAR`: `13/09/2026` isn't a date format the sniffer tries. **This isn't an error.** The file loads, and every date comparison on that column is now a string comparison: `min(createdAt)` returns `'13/09/2026 15:53'`, which would sort `01/10` before `30/09` as soon as the data spans two months.

`sniff_csv` also returns, in its `Prompt` column, the `read_csv` call that reproduces its guess, a starting point to fix by hand:

The fix here is to give [`read_csv`] the format ([lines 15-16]):

A wrong format fails the same silent way: with `timestampformat = '%m/%d/%Y %H:%M'` (month first), the column is `VARCHAR` again, with no message. To turn a wrong guess into an error, state the type as well, with `types = {'createdAt': 'TIMESTAMP'}`:

For a file that comes back every day, the SQL Server habit of a format file applies: write the `read_csv` call with `columns` or `types` once, and don't let the sniffer decide again each time.

## Parquet: types and columns

[Parquet] stores a table by column, compressed, with the schema. The JSON jobs file is 526,328 bytes; as Parquet, it's 37,270 bytes, 14 times smaller ([line 19]):

`parquet_metadata` shows what's inside, one row per column chunk ([lines 20-22]):

- Each field of the step struct is a column of its own. A query on step names reads the `steps, list, element, name` chunk and skips the timestamps: that's what "columnar" buys, and lesson 7 measures it.
- Timestamps are `INT64`: a number of microseconds, with the logical type in the schema. Strings are `BYTE_ARRAY`.
- 2,208 values for 2,204 steps: the 4 jobs with an empty `steps` list of lesson 3 still take one entry each, to record that the list is empty.
- The compression is [Snappy] by default; `COPY … (FORMAT parquet, COMPRESSION zstd)` selects another, and brings this file down to 24,243 bytes.

The script first compared `total_compressed_size` too. It passed on Linux and Windows, and failed on the macOS runner, an arm64 machine, where 8 of the 15 column chunks came out a few bytes different: `id` 1,652 bytes instead of 1,651, `name` 1,240 instead of 1,235, the step start times 8,862 instead of 8,864. Same data, same DuckDB version, different bytes. The checked output now keeps only what doesn't depend on the compressor.

## Many files: partitions and globs

`PARTITION_BY` writes one folder per value, named `column=value`, the layout known as [Hive partitioning] ([line 25]):

Sizes on Windows:

Without `OVERWRITE`, a second run of the script fails, unlike `COPY` to a single file, which replaces it without a word ([`physical_copy_to_file.cpp`]):

A glob reads all the files as one table. The `os` column isn't stored in the files: DuckDB sees the `key=value` folder names and [adds the column back]. `filename = true` adds the path of each row's file ([lines 28-31]):

The `replace` is there for the CI: file paths use the operating system's separator.

The glob pattern itself, `'out/jobs-by-os/*/*.parquet'`, works with forward slashes everywhere, Windows included.

## Files over HTTPS

A URL is a file name like any other. The copy of `runs.json` on GitHub ([lines 34-35]):

HTTP support is an [extension], [`httpfs`], not built into the CLI. With the default settings `autoinstall_known_extensions` and `autoload_known_extensions`, the first query that needs it downloads it, and later ones load it. It lands in the user's profile:

*To verify*: the path on Linux, deduced from the Windows one.

*To verify*: the path on macOS, deduced from the Windows one.

The CI of this course downloads it on each run, on each operating system, without any configuration. A machine without Internet access can't download it: run `INSTALL httpfs` ahead of time where the network is available. For Parquet over HTTP, DuckDB reads only the parts of the file it needs, with range requests: [lesson 7] counts the bytes.

## Key takeaways

- The CSV sniffer falls back to `VARCHAR` without a message; check with `sniff_csv` or `DESCRIBE`, and state the types of files you read regularly.
- Parquet keeps types and stores each column separately, nested fields included; it's the format to keep data in.
- `PARTITION_BY` writes `key=value` folders, a glob reads them back with the key as a column.
- File names in results use the OS separator; glob patterns accept `/` everywhere.
- `https://` paths need `httpfs`, which the CLI installs on first use.

## Exercises

The solutions are in [`sql/04-exercises.sql`], which writes the same files as the lesson so it runs on its own.

1. The spreadsheet format of `out/runs-fr.csv` lost information. Join the file back to `runs` and count the runs whose `createdAt` changed.

Solution

From [`sql/04-exercises.sql`, lines 10-12]:

All of them: `%H:%M` has no seconds, and none of the 125 runs started at `:00` seconds. The first run is `15:53:00` in the file and `15:53:16` in the JSON. A round trip through a spreadsheet format loses whatever the format can't write, silently again. `JOIN … USING (databaseId)` is the short form of `ON c.databaseId = r.databaseId` when both sides use the same name.

2. Count the Windows jobs and their failures, from the partitioned folder.

Solution

From [`sql/04-exercises.sql`, lines 15-18]:

The `os` column exists without `hive_partitioning = true`: DuckDB detected the folder layout. With `hive_partitioning = false`, it's gone:

According to the [documentation], a filter on a partition column skips the files of the other folders entirely: only `os=windows-latest` is opened. Lesson 7 checks it in the query plan.

3. `FROM 'data/*.json'` reads both JSON files of the course, which don't have the same fields. What does it return?

Solution

From [`sql/04-exercises.sql`, lines 21-25]:

No error: 440 rows and 20 columns, the union of both schemas. The fields of runs are `NULL` in the rows of jobs, and the other way around, and the fields both files have, `status` and `conclusion`, are merged into one column. Useful for files that gained a field over time; a trap when a glob catches a file it wasn't meant to. `count(column)` counts the non-`NULL` values, which is how the query tells the two schemas apart.

## Sources

- [CSV import] and [CSV auto-detection]
- [Parquet files] and [Parquet metadata]
- [Partitioned writes] and [Hive partitioning]
- [Reading multiple files]
- [Extensions] and [`httpfs`]
- [Apache Parquet]

pages.title: 5. DuckDB from C#
pages.body:
The CLI runs DuckDB in its own process. From C#, DuckDB runs **in your process**, as a native library called through [DuckDB.NET], an [ADO.NET] provider: `DbConnection`, `DbCommand`, `DbDataReader`, the classes you already use with SQL Server or SQLite. The program of this lesson is [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`], run from `code/duckdb` and compared with [`csharp/expected.txt`] on the three operating systems.

## The project

From [`csharp/CiQueries/CiQueries.csproj`, lines 10-13]:

DuckDB.NET comes in [four packages]: the ADO.NET provider (`DuckDB.NET.Data`) or the low-level bindings, each with or without the native DuckDB library. `.Full` includes it, for every platform, and that has a cost:

| | Size |
|---|---|
| `duckdb.net.bindings.full` 1.5.5 in the NuGet cache | 420 MB |
| `bin/Debug/net10.0` after `dotnet build` | 316 MB |
| `dotnet publish -r linux-x64` | 69 MB |

A plain build copies the native library of the five runtimes: `win-x64` (37 MB), `win-arm64` (43 MB), `linux-x64` (71 MB), `linux-arm64` (63 MB) and `osx` (117 MB, one file for Intel and Apple Silicon). Publishing for one runtime identifier keeps only its own. The package version follows DuckDB's: 1.5.5 embeds DuckDB 1.5.5.

## A query with a data reader

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 11-13]:

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 22-36]:

Nothing new for an ADO.NET user, and the SQL is the SQL of lesson 1, file name included. `Data Source=file.duckdb` opens or creates a database file instead; lesson 8 is about that.

`'data/runs.json'` is relative to the **working directory of the process**, not to the project or the executable. Run from the project folder with a `../data` path, the first version failed:

`../data` from `csharp/CiQueries` is `csharp/data`, which doesn't exist. An application that reads files should build absolute paths, from its configuration or `AppContext.BaseDirectory`.

## Parameters

DuckDB [accepts three syntaxes]: `?`, `$1` and `$name`. With `DuckDBParameter`, the name goes without the `$` ([lines 39-46]):

Even the file name is a parameter: `read_json($path)`, where SQL Server's `OPENROWSET(BULK …)` only takes a literal and pushes you to build the SQL string. A path that comes from a user still needs checking before it reaches `read_json`, since DuckDB can read any file the process can.

## DuckDB types as .NET types

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 49-69]:

- `DATE` becomes `DateOnly`, and `INTERVAL` becomes `TimeSpan`.
- `sum` of a `BIGINT` is a `HUGEINT`, a 128-bit integer, so `System.Numerics.BigInteger`, not `long`. Exercise 2 shows what that costs; `CAST(sum(…) AS BIGINT)` in the SQL avoids the question.
- A `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` comes back as a `DateTime` holding the UTC time, but with [`Kind`] `Unspecified`, not `Utc`. `ToUniversalTime()` treats an `Unspecified` value as local time and shifts it: in a scratch program on this machine (UTC−4), `15:53:16` became `19:53:16`, four hours off. `GetFieldValue` returns an explicit `+00:00`. The session's `TimeZone` setting of lesson 2 doesn't change what C# receives: with `SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Paris'`, the same `15:53:16` came back.
- The dates are formatted with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`: the first version printed `2026-09-14 2:01:09 PM` on this machine, a format that depends on the user's regional settings and would never match the CI's expected output.

## Lists and structs

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 72-88]:

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 174-182]:

- A `LIST` of `VARCHAR` reads as `List`; a `STRUCT` as a `Dictionary`, or as a class of yours.
- The mapping is by property name, ignoring case: `Started_At` matches `started_at`. **`StartedAt` doesn't, and nothing says so**: the property keeps its default value, `0001-01-01`. In C#, the natural name is the one that silently fails. Rename in SQL (exercise 1), or check the defaults in a test.
- A positional `record Step(long Number, …)` fails at run time: `MissingMethodException: Cannot dynamically create an instance of type 'Step'. Reason: No parameterless constructor defined.` The target type needs a parameterless constructor and setters, or `init` accessors.

## Errors

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, lines 91-103]:

One exception type, `DuckDBException`, with the same message as the CLI, suggestions and position included. Its `ErrorType` says `Invalid`, not `Binder`: to tell error kinds apart, the message prefix is more precise than the property. The command stays usable after the error: in a scratch program, the same `DuckDBCommand` then ran `SELECT 42` and returned `42`. Lesson 6 shows that the Java driver behaves differently.

## Dapper

[Dapper] extends any `DbConnection`, so it works on `DuckDBConnection` without an adapter ([lines 106-118]):

From [`csharp/CiQueries/Program.cs`, line 171]:

The properties of the anonymous object become the `$conclusion` and `$event` parameters; `@event` is how C# writes a property named after a keyword. Unlike DuckDB.NET's struct mapping, Dapper fills a positional record through its constructor. The three failed pushes are the Rust course failures of lesson 2.

## Bulk loading: the appender

Loading rows one `INSERT` at a time is slow in every database. DuckDB.NET exposes DuckDB's [appender], which writes rows straight into a table's storage ([lines 138-146]):

The program's `timings` mode loads a million rows with the appender, then 10,000 rows with a parameterized `INSERT` in a transaction. The CI prints the timings without comparing them:

| Runner | Appender, 1,000,000 rows | `INSERT`, 10,000 rows |
|---|---|---|
| `ubuntu-latest` | 256 ms | 3,165 ms |
| `windows-latest` | 331 ms | 3,917 ms |
| `macos-latest` | 226 ms | 1,312 ms |
| This machine (Windows, Release) | 170 ms | 1,577 ms |

With 100 times more rows, the appender is still 6 to 12 times faster: per row, 600 to 1,200 times faster. The rows are written when the appender is disposed, hence the `using`: in a scratch program, `count(*)` on the table was `0` after appending 10 rows, and `10` after `Dispose()`. For data already in a file, `INSERT INTO … SELECT * FROM 'file.parquet'` is simpler still and doesn't cross the managed/native boundary for each value.

## Key takeaways

- DuckDB.NET is an ADO.NET provider: `DuckDBConnection`, commands, readers, transactions and Dapper work as with any other database.
- The `.Full` package embeds the native library of every platform; publish for a runtime identifier to ship one.
- Relative file paths in SQL are relative to the process's working directory.
- `DATE` → `DateOnly`, `INTERVAL` → `TimeSpan`, `HUGEINT` → `BigInteger`, `TIMESTAMPTZ` → `DateTime` with `Kind` `Unspecified`.
- Structs map to classes by property name, and an unmatched property silently keeps its default.
- For many rows, use the appender, or let DuckDB read the file.

## Exercises

1. Change the `Step` class so that `StartedAt` gets the step's start time without renaming it, by changing only the SQL.

Solution

Rebuild each struct with the names the class expects, with `list_transform` from lesson 3:

With a `Step` class that only has `Number`, `Name` and `StartedAt`, the first step reads:

The SQL becomes the one place where the external format (the GitHub API's `snake_case`) meets the C# naming. This check was run once in a scratch program, not in the CI program.

2. `ExecuteScalar` on `SELECT sum(databaseId) FROM 'data/runs.json'` returns an `object`. What's its type, and what does `(long)command.ExecuteScalar()!` do?

Solution

`sum` of a `BIGINT` is a `HUGEINT`, read as `System.Numerics.BigInteger` (section 3 of the program). The cast throws:

Unboxing only works to the exact boxed type. The usual escape, `Convert.ToInt64(value)`, fails too, because `BigInteger` doesn't implement `IConvertible`:

What works: unbox to the real type, then convert, `(long)(BigInteger)value`, which gave `4351672497299`; or `CAST(sum(databaseId) AS BIGINT)` in SQL, so that the reader returns a `long`. Checked in a scratch program, not in the CI program.

3. Why does section 5 print `e.Message.Split('\n')[0]` rather than the whole message?

Solution

The full message has several lines, like in the CLI: the error, `Candidate bindings: "workflowName", "conclusion"`, a blank line, then the query with a `^` under the position. The first line is enough for a log and keeps the expected output short. Keep the full message where a developer reads it: the position marker is the most useful part of a syntax error in a long query.

## Sources

- [DuckDB.NET documentation]: [getting started] and [basic usage]
- [DuckDB.NET source code]
- [`DuckDB.NET.Data.Full` on NuGet]
- [DuckDB clients overview] and [appender]
- [Dapper]
- [ADO.NET overview]

pages.title: 6. DuckDB from Java
pages.body:
The same program as [lesson 5], in Java, with the [DuckDB JDBC driver]: [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`], compared with [`java/expected.txt`] on the three operating systems. The differences with C# are the interesting part.

## The project

From [`java/pom.xml`, lines 20-26]:

One artifact, [`org.duckdb:duckdb_jdbc`], versioned after DuckDB with a fourth number for driver releases: 1.5.5.1 embeds DuckDB 1.5.5. The jar is 85 MB, because it contains the native library for four platforms:

Where DuckDB.NET splits platforms into NuGet runtime folders, the JDBC driver ships one jar for all, and picks the right file at run time. There's no Windows on Arm build in this list.

The program runs with the [Exec Maven Plugin], from `code/duckdb` so that `data/…` paths resolve, like in C#:

## A query with a result set

From [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`, line 21]:

From [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`, lines 33-44]:

`jdbc:duckdb:` with nothing after the colon is an in-memory database; `jdbc:duckdb:ci.duckdb` opens a file. The output is the same as the C# program's, character for character, apart from the section title.

## Parameters

From [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`, lines 47-56]:

JDBC's `?` placeholders, numbered from 1. The file path is a parameter here too.

## DuckDB types as Java types

The same query as in C#:

Side by side with lesson 5:

| DuckDB | C# (DuckDB.NET) | Java (JDBC) |
|---|---|---|
| `TIMESTAMP` | `DateTime` | `java.sql.Timestamp`, or `LocalDateTime` with `getObject(i, LocalDateTime.class)` |
| `DATE` | `DateOnly` | `LocalDate` |
| `INTERVAL` | `TimeSpan` | **`String`** |
| `TIMESTAMPTZ` | `DateTime`, UTC value, `Kind` `Unspecified` | `OffsetDateTime` **in the JVM's time zone** |
| `HUGEINT` | `BigInteger` | `BigInteger` |
| `LIST` | `List` | `java.sql.Array` |
| `STRUCT` | `Dictionary` or a class | `java.sql.Struct` (`DuckDBStruct`) |

- `INTERVAL` arrives as the text `00:00:39`. To compute with it, convert in SQL (`epoch(took)` gives seconds as a `DOUBLE`) rather than parsing the string.
- `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` becomes an [`OffsetDateTime`] expressed in the JVM's default zone. The same instant printed on this machine with `getObject(i).toString()`: `2026-09-13T11:53:16-04:00`; with `-Duser.timezone=UTC`: `2026-09-13T15:53:16Z`. DuckDB's own `SET TimeZone` or a `TimeZone` connection property changed nothing in the Java value. That's why the program prints `toInstant()` and `withOffsetSameInstant(ZoneOffset.UTC)`, which don't depend on where it runs.

## Arrays and structs

From [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`, lines 80-91]:

JDBC predates generics in this area: [`Array.getArray()`] returns an `Object` to cast, and a struct is a [`java.sql.Struct`] whose standard `getAttributes()` gives the values by position only. The driver's `DuckDBStruct.getMap()` adds the names, at the price of a cast to a driver class. There's no mapping to a record or a class: that's the job of a library like Spring's `JdbcTemplate` or jOOQ, *not tried in this course*.

## Errors: a statement that closes itself

From [`java/src/main/java/ci/CiQueries.java`, lines 94-109]:

Three differences with C#:

- The message starts with a generic line, `Attempting to execute an unsuccessful or closed pending query result`, and the actual error comes on the second line, after `Error: `. A log that keeps only the first line of the message keeps nothing useful.
- `SQLState` is `null`: code that checks SQL states, such as a retry on `40001`, gets nothing from this driver.
- **The statement is closed after the error.** In C#, the same `DuckDBCommand` ran the next query. In Java, a loop that reuses one `Statement` and catches errors to continue fails on every query after the first error, with `Statement was closed`. Create a statement per query, which `try`-with-resources makes natural.

## Native access on JDK 25

Through Maven, the program prints nothing but its output. Run directly with `java`, it starts with four warnings:

*To verify*: run on Windows only; the classpath separator is `:` outside Windows.

*To verify*: run on Windows only; the classpath separator is `:` outside Windows.

Loading a native library is a "restricted method" since [JEP 472]: a warning today, an error in a future JDK. `java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -cp …` removes the warnings. Maven didn't show them because its launch script already passes that option to the JVM it runs in (`bin/mvn`, Maven 3.9.16), and `exec:java` runs the program inside that JVM. A packaged application must add the option to its own launch command.

## Bulk loading

The `timings` mode loads a million rows with the driver's appender, then 10,000 rows with a batch and with single `INSERT` statements, in a transaction ([lines 120-127]):

`unwrap` is the JDBC way to reach a driver's own class from a `Connection`. The CI timings, with the C# ones of lesson 5 for comparison:

| Runner | Java appender, 1,000,000 rows | Java batch, 10,000 rows | Java one by one, 10,000 rows | C# `INSERT`, 10,000 rows |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ubuntu-latest` | 257 ms | 858 ms | 832 ms | 3,165 ms |
| `windows-latest` | 511 ms | 2,443 ms | 2,378 ms | 3,917 ms |
| `macos-latest` | 212 ms | 690 ms | 675 ms | 1,312 ms |

- The appender loads a million rows in about the time C# takes, apart from Windows.
- `addBatch` and `executeBatch` bring nothing: the batch was no faster than single statements on any runner, or on this machine (609 ms against 532 ms). With this driver, a JDBC batch doesn't send the rows in one call. Use the appender, or `INSERT … SELECT` from a file.
- The single `INSERT` statements are 1.6 to 3.8 times faster in Java than in C#. *Not investigated*: both prepare the statement once; the difference may be in how each wrapper binds parameters.

## Key takeaways

- One jar, `org.duckdb:duckdb_jdbc`, holds the driver and the native libraries of four platforms; the JDBC URL `jdbc:duckdb:` opens an in-memory database.
- `INTERVAL` is a `String`, and `TIMESTAMPTZ` an `OffsetDateTime` in the JVM's zone: convert to an `Instant` before printing or comparing.
- Arrays and structs go through `java.sql.Array` and `DuckDBStruct.getMap()`, with casts.
- After an error, the statement is closed: one statement per query.
- JDK 25 warns about native access unless the JVM is started with `--enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED`.
- JDBC batches don't speed up inserts with this driver; the appender does.

## Exercises

1. A service runs `SELECT createdAt AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' FROM runs` and returns `rs.getObject(1).toString()` in a JSON response. It gives `2026-09-13T15:53:16Z` in production and `2026-09-13T11:53:16-04:00` on a developer's laptop. Is one of them wrong? How do you make them agree?

Solution

Neither is wrong: both are the same instant, with different offsets. The value depends on the JVM's default time zone (`user.timezone`, or the OS setting), as the lesson measured. To make the output independent of the machine, choose the representation in code: `rs.getObject(1, OffsetDateTime.class).toInstant()` prints `2026-09-13T15:53:16Z` everywhere, and so does `withOffsetSameInstant(ZoneOffset.UTC)`. Starting the JVM with `-Duser.timezone=UTC` also works, but it changes every date of the application, and it's easy to forget on one machine.

2. This loop inserts rows and skips the invalid ones. With the DuckDB driver, what happens after the first invalid row?

Solution

Every following statement fails with `Statement was closed`, and the loop "skips" all the remaining rows, valid or not: section 5 of the program shows the statement closed after a failed query. Create the statement inside the loop:

Checked in a scratch program with three `INSERT` statements, the second one inserting `'x'` into an `INTEGER` column:

The third row, valid, was never inserted.

3. The C# program formats dates with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`. Does the Java program have the same problem with `printf("%,d")` in its `timings` mode, and does it matter for the CI?

Solution

Yes: `%,d` uses the default locale's grouping separator. The CI printed `1,000,000`; in a scratch program, `String.format(Locale.FRANCE, "%,d", 1_000_000)` separated the groups with U+202F, a narrow no-break space, which looks like a space and isn't one for a parser. It doesn't matter for the CI, because `check.sh` only compares the `check` mode's output, and the timings aren't compared. For output that is compared or parsed, use `String.format(Locale.ROOT, …)`, which gave `1,000,000`.

## Sources

- [DuckDB Java (JDBC) client], [connecting], [querying], [result handling] and [data import]
- [DuckDB Java source code]
- [`org.duckdb:duckdb_jdbc` on Maven Central]
- [JEP 472: Prepare to Restrict the Use of JNI]
- [`java.sql` package]
- [Exec Maven Plugin]

pages.title: 7. Performance
pages.body:
In SQL Server, you read an [execution plan] to see why a query is slow, and a [columnstore index] is what makes analytical scans fast. DuckDB stores everything in columns, and has plans too. This lesson reads them, then measures what they predict.

Two scripts:

- [`sql/07-performance.sql`] shows plans and Parquet metadata. Its output doesn't depend on the machine, so the CI compares it like the other lessons.
- [`timings/07-performance.sql`] runs the same ideas on a bigger table with `.timer on`. The CI runs it on the three operating systems without comparing anything; the timings below come from its logs and from my machine, a 24-thread Windows 11 PC.

It writes about 1.5 GB into `out/`: a 1 GB CSV file and several Parquet files. Delete them afterwards.

## A bigger table

315 jobs are not enough to measure anything. The script repeats every step of every job, shifting the timestamps by one day per copy ([lines 7-11]):

`range(500)` is a table function that returns the numbers 0 to 499; the comma joins it to every step. The timings script uses `range(5000)`: 11,020,000 steps, created in 1.1 s on my machine and between 2.0 s (Ubuntu runner) and 4.0 s (Windows runner) in the CI.

## Reading a plan

[`EXPLAIN`] shows the physical plan without running the query. Here, a query on the JSON file ([line 18]):

Read it from the bottom up, like a SQL Server plan read from right to left: the scan produces rows for the operator above it. The numbers with `~` are the optimizer's estimates; `#0` is the first column of the operator below. The estimate for the groups, 199, is far from the real four conclusions: it doesn't matter much here, but when a join is slow, a wrong estimate is the first thing to look for.

The line to notice is `Projections: conclusion`. The jobs have 11 fields, including the `steps` array; the reader only builds the one column the query uses. That is **projection pushdown**. With JSON, the reader still has to parse the whole text to find that field. With Parquet, it doesn't even read the other columns.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and adds the real row counts and the time spent in each operator. The [profiling documentation] lists the other outputs, such as JSON.

## Filter pushdown and row groups

The script writes the steps twice: `out/steps.parquet` in insertion order, `out/steps-sorted.parquet` sorted by start time.

From [`sql/07-performance.sql`, lines 14-25]:

Three columns out of seven, and a `Filters:` section: the `WHERE` clause moved into the scan. That is **filter pushdown**, and on Parquet it does more than save a filter operator.

A [Parquet file] is cut into **row groups**; DuckDB writes one every 122,880 rows. For each column of each row group, the footer of the file stores the minimum and the maximum value. Before reading a row group, the scan compares the filter with those statistics, and skips the row group if no row can match. [`parquet_metadata`] shows them ([lines 28-33]):

Same rows, same answer (13,895 steps for both files), but not the same work. In insertion order, every row group mixes steps from the whole period, so every minimum falls in the first week and no row group can be skipped. Sorted, only the first row group starts before 2026-09-20.

The plan is the same for both files: `EXPLAIN` shows that the filter reaches the scan, not how many row groups it will skip. The timings show it. One thread, one day in 2030, on the 11-million-row files:

| One day, one thread | My machine | Ubuntu runner | Windows runner | macOS runner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| unsorted Parquet | 0.052 s | 0.061 s | 0.098 s | 0.059 s |
| sorted Parquet | 0.003 s | 0.003 s | 0.007 s | 0.007 s |

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the sorted file confirms that the scan produced only the matching rows, from one file:

DuckDB's own tables work the same way: the [indexing guide] calls these per-row-group statistics *zonemaps*, and says that "the more ordered the data within a column, the more valuable the zonemap indexes will be". If a column is filtered often, sort by it when you write the file. Sorting also compresses better: the sorted 11-million-row file was 106 MB against 119 MB on my machine.

:::note[File sizes change between runs]
The Parquet writer uses several threads, and the sizes changed by a few hundred kilobytes between two runs on the same machine, and by a few megabytes between machines: the sorted file was 102 MB on the three runners. That's why the compared script shows row counts and statistics, never compressed sizes.
:::

## Partition pruning

Lesson 4 said that a filter on a partition column skips whole files. `EXPLAIN` shows it without running anything ([line 41]):

`File Filters` are decided from the folder names alone: the other two files aren't opened. [Hive partitioning] is to files what row group statistics are to rows.

## Table, Parquet or CSV

The same aggregate, the slowest step on average, on the 11 million steps stored three ways, with every thread ([`timings/07-performance.sql`, line 19]):

| Source | My machine (24 threads) | Ubuntu (4) | Windows (4) | macOS (3) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `steps` table in memory | 0.042 s | 0.263 s | 0.420 s | 0.289 s |
| `out/steps-big.parquet`, 119 MB | 0.048 s | 0.237 s | 0.553 s | 0.415 s |
| `out/steps-big.csv`, 1.09 GB | 0.416 s | 1.676 s | 2.709 s | 2.403 s |
| filter on one week, Parquet | 0.009 s | 0.025 s | 0.034 s | 0.026 s |
| filter on one week, CSV | 0.383 s | 1.064 s | 1.698 s | 1.117 s |

Every query returned the same row: `Lesson 10 builds` on `windows-latest`, 2 min 24.75 s. Parquet is as fast as a table in memory, because DuckDB reads only three columns and decodes them in bulk. CSV is 5 to 9 times slower than Parquet on the aggregate: every value is text to parse, and there are no statistics, so the week filter reads the whole gigabyte. Writing took 0.41 s for Parquet and 0.50 s for CSV on my machine. If a CSV file is queried more than once, convert it first.

## Threads

DuckDB runs a query on as many threads as the machine has cores: the [`threads` setting] defaults to the number of CPU cores. The runners showed 4, 4 and 3. The aggregate on the table, with `SET threads = 1`:

| Aggregate on the table | My machine | Ubuntu | Windows | macOS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all threads | 0.042 s | 0.263 s | 0.420 s | 0.289 s |
| `SET threads = 1` | 0.530 s | 0.632 s | 1.089 s | 1.120 s |

12.6 times faster with 24 threads, 2.4 to 3.9 times with 3 or 4. Scans and hash aggregates split well across threads. The other side: a DuckDB query in a web server takes every core by default, and several at once compete for them. Set `threads` when DuckDB shares the machine.

## A remote Parquet file

Lesson 4 read Parquet over HTTPS and claimed that DuckDB downloads only what it needs. The [HTTP log] proves it, on January 2024 of the [New York City taxi trips], a 49,961,641-byte file ([`timings/07-performance.sql`, lines 46-49]):

Enabling the log prints a warning in the CLI, because the log now also collects warnings:

The script repeats the count for two other queries. The downloads were the same on my machine and on the three runners:

| Query | Result | `GET` requests | Bytes downloaded | Time, my machine |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `count(*)` | 2,964,624 | 1 | 65,536 | 0.25 s |
| `avg(trip_distance)` | 3.6521691789583146 | 3 | 4,082,947 | 0.63 s |
| `SELECT * … LIMIT 1` | one trip | 1 | 17,612,330 | 1.64 s |

Every query starts with a `HEAD` request for the file size. The first one then downloads the end of the file, where the footer is, and needs nothing else: the row counts are in the footer. The average reads one column, the `LIMIT 1` reads every column of one row group. Exercise 3 matches these numbers with the metadata.

On a network, the column layout matters more than on a disk: `SELECT *` on a remote file is the expensive query, even with `LIMIT 1`.

## Memory and spilling to disk

By default, DuckDB may use 80% of the RAM (`memory_limit`). When a sort, a join, a `GROUP BY` or a window function needs more, the [tuning guide] says that it spills to temporary files, in `temp_directory`: `.tmp` next to the process for an in-memory database, `.tmp` next to a database file. The timings script sorts the 11 million steps from the Parquet file under two limits ([`timings/07-performance.sql`, lines 59-64]):

| Sort of 11 million rows | My machine | Ubuntu | Windows | macOS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500 MB, all threads | 2.21 s | 2.91 s | 4.62 s | 4.92 s |
| 100 MB, one thread | 6.34 s | 6.96 s | 9.89 s | 7.94 s |

On my machine, the same sort took 1.37 s with 1 GB. With 100 MB and four threads, it failed:

Threads work in parallel, each on its own part of the data, so fewer threads need less memory at the same time: that is the first suggestion, and it's why the script sets one thread. The failed `COPY` also left a file behind: 1.1 MB in one run; empty in another, where the next query failed with `File 'out/steps-big-sorted-100mb.parquet' too small to be a Parquet file`. Check that a `COPY` succeeded before using its file.

Two traps seen along the way. Lowering the limit below what is already used fails: in a session holding the 11-million-row table, `SET memory_limit = '10MB'` answered `Failed to change memory limit to 10000000: could not free up enough memory for the new limit`. And a table in an in-memory database counts in the limit too: after `SET memory_limit = '100MB'` in that session, queries failed with `failed to pin block`. That's why the script drops the table first.

## When DuckDB is the wrong tool

DuckDB is [designed for analytical queries]: a few large scans, aggregates and joins. What this course measured, and what the documentation says, points to other tools for:

- **Many small transactions.** An `INSERT` per row took 0.07 to 0.4 ms in the CI of lessons 5 and 6, where the appender loaded a million rows in 0.2 to 0.5 s. An order-entry system belongs in SQL Server or PostgreSQL.
- **Several processes writing to the same database.** One process can read and write a database file; [several processes can only read it]. Lesson 8 tries it.
- **A shared server for many users.** DuckDB lives inside your process; there is no server, no users and no permissions to manage.
- **A database file on a network share.** The [FAQ] strongly advises against read-write workloads on network-attached storage.

For reading files, a CI history, a data export or a notebook, it's the right size.

## Key takeaways

- `EXPLAIN` shows the plan; read it from the bottom up. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and adds real rows and times.
- `Projections:` in a scan is the list of columns actually read; `Filters:` is the part of the `WHERE` clause pushed into the scan.
- Parquet row groups carry min/max statistics per column. A filter skips row groups only if the data is ordered on that column: sort files by the column you filter on.
- Partition folders are skipped before any file is opened (`Scanning Files: 1/3`).
- Parquet is about as fast as an in-memory table, and 5 to 9 times faster than CSV for these queries.
- DuckDB uses every core by default; set `threads` when it shares a machine.
- A remote Parquet query downloads the footer and the column chunks it needs; `SELECT *` downloads whole row groups.
- With a memory limit, sorts, joins and aggregates spill to `temp_directory`; each thread needs memory, so reduce `threads` for small limits.

## Exercises

The solutions are in [`sql/07-exercises.sql`]; their timings are in the timings script.

1. Four ways to keep the steps of 2030-01-01, on the sorted file. Which ones can skip row groups? Does `EXPLAIN` tell you?

From [`timings/07-performance.sql`, lines 34-37]:

Solution

`EXPLAIN` shows a `Filters:` section in the scan for all four, so it doesn't answer. But what it shows differs. On the small file, with 2026-09-14, the cast and `date_trunc` were rewritten into a range:

The `strftime` filter stays an expression, which no min/max statistic can answer:

The timings agree. All four return 2,204 steps; with one thread, the range, the cast and `date_trunc` took 0.002 to 0.005 s on my machine and on the runners, while `strftime` took 0.467 s on my machine, and 0.60 s (Ubuntu), 0.96 s (macOS) and 1.12 s (Windows) in the CI, because it formats 11 million timestamps as text. In SQL Server, wrapping a column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable; DuckDB's optimizer undoes some of those wrappers, not all. Compare columns with values of their own type.

2. The steps are filtered by `os = 'windows-latest'`. How many of the 9 row groups must be read in `out/steps.parquet`, in `out/steps-sorted.parquet`, and in a file sorted by `os, started_at`?

Solution

Write the third file, then compare the filter with the `os` statistics ([`sql/07-exercises.sql`, lines 16-22]):

Sorting by time helps time filters and nothing else. A file can be sorted well for one column only, or for a leading column and, inside each value, the next one. For a column with a few values like `os`, partitioning (one folder per value) is another answer.

3. Explain the bytes downloaded by the three remote queries (65,536, then 4,082,947, then 17,612,330) with `parquet_metadata` on the same URL.

Solution

From [`sql/07-exercises.sql`, lines 25-29]:

- `count(*)`: 65,536 bytes is one range request of 64 KiB at the end of the file. The footer fits in it, and the row counts (1,048,576 + 1,048,576 + 867,472 = 2,964,624) are in the footer.
- `avg(trip_distance)`: 1,441,439 + 1,451,920 + 1,189,588 = 4,082,947, exactly the three `trip_distance` chunks, one request per row group. There was no request for the footer: it was already in DuckDB's cache of remote files (`enable_external_file_cache`, `true` by default), from the first query of the session.
- `SELECT * … LIMIT 1`: every column of row group 0, 17,611,010 bytes, plus 1,320 bytes. A range request covers contiguous bytes: from byte 4, where the first chunk starts after the `PAR1` magic number, to the end of the last chunk. In the metadata, `dictionary_page_offset` and `total_compressed_size` give that span, 17,612,330 bytes; the 1,320 bytes are the gaps between the chunks of the 19 columns.

## Sources

- [`EXPLAIN`], [`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`] and [profiling]
- [Performance guide]: [file formats], [indexing], [tuning workloads]
- [Parquet metadata] and [Parquet tips]
- [Apache Parquet file format]
- [Configuration settings]: `threads`, `memory_limit`, `temp_directory`
- [Logging]
- [Hive partitioning]
- [Concurrency], [Why DuckDB] and the [FAQ]
- [TLC Trip Record Data], New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission

pages.title: 8. Persistence, transactions and concurrency
pages.body:
Until now, the tables lived in memory and vanished with the process, and the files were CSV, JSON or Parquet. This lesson keeps the data in a DuckDB database file, then does what an application does with a database: transactions, constraints, and more than one connection or process at a time.

Two programs, compared by the CI on the three operating systems like the queries of the other lessons:

- [`shell/08-persistence.sh`] runs the DuckDB CLI several times, sometimes two processes at once, and prints file sizes and exit codes. Its output is compared with [`shell/expected/08-persistence.txt`].
- [`java/src/main/java/ci/Transactions.java`] opens two JDBC connections to the same file, compared with [`java/expected-transactions.txt`].

In the script, `run` is the DuckDB CLI in CSV mode followed by its exit code, and `files` prints the size of each file.

## A database file

Give the CLI a file name, and the tables go into that file ([lines 49-51]):

One file, `out/ci.duckdb`, for all the tables, like an SQLite file rather than a SQL Server `.mdf`. [`pragma_database_size`] shows how it's organized: blocks of 262,144 bytes (256 KiB), three of them here, plus 12,288 bytes before the first block. The file grows by whole blocks.

In a program, [`ATTACH`] opens a database file next to the in-memory database, and a query can join tables from both. `ATTACH` also chooses the storage format ([line 52]):

DuckDB 1.5.5 still writes files in the 1.0.0 format by default, so that older versions can read them: the [storage page] says that versions 1.0 to 1.5 all create storage version 64 by default. I checked it with the DuckDB 1.0.0 CLI, which isn't part of the CI, on two files created the same way: it read the default one, and refused the `v1.5.0` one:

The rest of that message still says that the storage format isn't stable yet and will be with version 1.0, which is the version printing it. Keep the default when a file is shared with other tools or other DuckDB versions.

## The write-ahead log

A committed change isn't written into the blocks right away. DuckDB appends it to a write-ahead log, a second file named after the database with `.wal` added, and moves it into the database file at a **checkpoint**: when the log reaches 16 MiB (`checkpoint_threshold`), on [`CHECKPOINT`], and when the database is closed. The script turns off the checkpoint on close to see the log ([lines 55-58]):

After the first process, the database file hasn't changed and the 2,204 steps are only in the 135,677-byte log. The second process replayed the log when it opened the file, and checkpointed when it closed it: one more block, no more log. The `.wal` file plays the role of the [SQL Server transaction log], but it only lives until the next checkpoint: there are no log backups or log truncation to manage.

The consequence for backups: a copy of `ci.duckdb` alone can miss committed data. In a scratch test, a copy made while the log existed opened without its last table; with the `.wal` file copied next to it, the table was there. Copy both files, or run `CHECKPOINT` first, or close the database.

## Free blocks and compaction

From [`shell/08-persistence.sh`, lines 61-64]:

Dropping `jobs` freed a block in the middle of the file: DuckDB reuses it for the next writes, but the file keeps its size. In an earlier version of the script, I dropped `steps`, the last table written, and the file shrank back to 798,720 bytes: free blocks at the end of the file are cut off. To get the space back in any case, [`COPY FROM DATABASE`] copies every table into a new file.

## Transactions

Each statement runs in its own transaction, unless you open one with `BEGIN` ([lines 68-79]):

Three things to read in this output:

- `CREATE TABLE` is transactional: the rollback removed the table too.
- The first error aborted the whole transaction. The following `SELECT` was refused, and the valid `INSERT` before the error was lost.
- **`COMMIT` of an aborted transaction printed no error.** It rolled back, silently: the table doesn't exist afterwards. The only signal in the CLI is the exit code, 1 because of the earlier errors. The Java program below shows the same behaviour through JDBC.

A SQL Server developer expects something else: with [`SET XACT_ABORT OFF`], the default, a constraint violation rolls back only the statement, and `COMMIT` commits the rest. In DuckDB, check every statement of a transaction, and don't trust a `COMMIT` that didn't throw.

The [transactions page] gives the isolation level: snapshot isolation. A transaction sees the database as it was when the transaction started.

## Constraints and upserts

From [`shell/08-persistence.sh`, lines 84-90]:

The same violation has two messages: `Duplicate key "name: builds" violates primary key constraint` for a single statement, and `PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint violation: duplicate key "builds"` inside a transaction in the previous section. Don't match on the text.

Where SQL Server has `MERGE`, DuckDB has [`INSERT … ON CONFLICT`], as in PostgreSQL: `excluded` is the row that was refused. `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `INSERT OR IGNORE` are the SQLite shortcuts for `DO UPDATE` on every column and `DO NOTHING`. They need a primary key or a unique [constraint] to detect the conflict.

## Two connections in one process

Two `DriverManager.getConnection` calls with the same file name share one database: the second connection sees the table the first one created. Each connection has its own transaction ([`java/src/main/java/ci/Transactions.java`, lines 21-35]):

`execute` prints the first value of the result, `ok`, or the error on one line:

In SQL Server, with the default locking behaviour, `b`'s `UPDATE` would wait for `a` to commit, then apply. DuckDB uses optimistic concurrency control: `b` fails at once with `Conflict on update!`, its transaction is aborted, and `commit()` returns without an exception, like the CLI's `COMMIT`. The counter ends at 1, not 2: one increment was lost, and only the error on the `UPDATE` tells you. The [concurrency page] suggests running the transaction again; that's exercise 2.

Inserts behave differently:

Appends to the same table don't conflict. A duplicate key between two transactions isn't detected at the `INSERT`, but at the second commit, which throws this time.

The C# driver wraps the same engine, so the behaviour should be the same with DuckDB.NET; the C# program of lesson 5 doesn't test it (*to verify*).

## Two processes

Within a process, many connections. Between processes, the rule is simpler: the script keeps the database open in a background CLI process, then starts a second one.

From [`shell/08-persistence.sh`, lines 94-96]:

Both attempts fail, even the read-only one, and even though the first process isn't writing anything. The message depends on the operating system, so the script compares only the error type and the exit code, and prints the full message on the error output. From the CI logs and my machine ([`local_file_system.cpp`: Windows], [Linux, macOS]):

All three name the process that holds the file, which helps when a forgotten CLI or an IDE keeps it open. The Linux / WSL tab comes from the Ubuntu runner, not from WSL.

Processes that open the file read-only, with `-readonly` in the CLI, can share it ([lines 103-106]):

A second reader works, a read-only process can't write, and a process that wants to write can't open the file while a reader has it. On Linux and macOS, that last message adds a hint: `However, you would be able to open this database in read-only mode, e.g. by using the -readonly parameter in the CLI.` With JDBC, the `duckdb.read_only` property set to `true` in the connection properties opened the file read-only in a scratch program, and refused an `INSERT` with the same message.

So a DuckDB file has either **one process that reads and writes**, with as many connections and threads as it wants inside, or **several processes that only read**. The [concurrency page] lists two ways around it for several writing processes, neither tested in this course: the Quack remote protocol, which turns DuckDB into a client-server database and is in beta in 1.5; and [DuckLake], which stores the catalog in a database such as PostgreSQL and the data in Parquet files. And the [FAQ] strongly advises against read-write workloads on network-attached storage.

## Key takeaways

- A database file is made of 256 KiB blocks; `pragma_database_size` shows them, and a freed block is reused but doesn't shrink the file unless it's at the end. `COPY FROM DATABASE` compacts.
- New files use the 1.0.0 storage format by default, readable by DuckDB 1.0; `STORAGE_VERSION` opts into newer formats.
- Committed changes go first to the `.wal` file, and into the database at a checkpoint. Back up both files, or checkpoint first.
- The first error aborts a transaction, and `COMMIT` then rolls back without an error, in the CLI and in JDBC.
- `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`, `INSERT OR REPLACE` and `INSERT OR IGNORE` handle duplicate keys.
- Concurrency is optimistic: a second update of the same row fails at once, a duplicate key fails at commit, appends don't conflict. Retry the transaction.
- One process may open a file for writing, and then no other process can open it; or several processes may open it read-only.

## Exercises

1. The DuckDB CLI runs three statements in one `-c` argument; the third one violates the primary key. How many rows are left? And with `BEGIN;` and `COMMIT;` around them?

From [`shell/08-exercises.sh`, line 10]:

Solution

From [`shell/08-exercises.sh`]:

Two rows: each statement committed on its own, and only the failing one was lost. The [transactions page] says that statements submitted together run in a single implicit transaction and are all rolled back if one fails; that isn't what the CLI did with DuckDB 1.5.5, nor JDBC, where `statement.execute` with the same three statements also left two rows in a scratch program. With `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, the error aborted the transaction, `COMMIT` rolled it back silently, and no row was left. When several statements must succeed together, write the transaction explicitly.

2. In section 2 of the Java program, `b` loses its increment. Change the end of the section so that the counter ends at 2.

Solution

After the conflict, roll `b` back, then run its transaction again once `a` has committed:

In a scratch program with the same sequence, starting from 1, the counter ended at 3: both increments applied. In a real program, the retry is a loop around the whole transaction, reading the row again, because the value `b` read before the conflict is stale. Retry only on write conflicts such as `Conflict on update!`: a duplicate key at commit is also a `TransactionContext Error`, and retrying it fails every time. The `SQLState` is null with this driver (lesson 6), so the message is all you have.

3. Your ASP.NET Core API runs on two instances behind a load balancer, and both are meant to insert CI runs into `ci.duckdb` on a shared disk. What happens, and what would you do?

Solution

The first instance to open the file gets it; the second fails at startup or at its first query with `IO Error`, as in the two-process section, and so would any other process, even a read-only one, as long as the first instance keeps the file open. A shared network disk makes it worse: the FAQ advises against read-write workloads there.

Options, from simplest:

- one writer: a single process owns the file and the other instances send it their inserts, through an API or a queue;
- each instance writes its own files (Parquet or its own DuckDB file), and a reader queries them all with a glob, as in lesson 4;
- open, write and close quickly, and retry when the file is locked: two processes run one after the other without problem, but they fail under load (*to verify* at scale);
- if the data really is transactional and shared, a server database such as PostgreSQL or SQL Server, possibly with DuckDB reading from it for analytics; DuckLake and Quack are the DuckDB answers, not tested here.

## Sources

- [Concurrency] and [transactions]
- [`ATTACH`], [`CHECKPOINT`], [`COPY FROM DATABASE`]
- [Storage versions and compatibility]
- [Pragmas]: `database_size`, `disable_checkpoint_on_shutdown`
- [`INSERT`] and [constraints]
- [CLI arguments], including `-readonly`
- [DuckLake] and the [DuckDB FAQ]
- SQL Server: [transaction log], [`SET XACT_ABORT`], [locking and row versioning]

pages.title: DuckDB — Mission
pages.body:
:::note[How this course is tested]
Every query in this course is in [`code/duckdb/sql`], next to its expected output. [`.github/workflows/duckdb-examples.yml`] runs them all with the DuckDB CLI on Linux, Windows and macOS and compares the results. The outputs in the lessons were captured with DuckDB 1.5.5 in September 2026.
:::

## Why I'm learning this

Every question I ask about the CI of this site — which workflow fails most, how long the Windows jobs take, which step got slower — ends in a pile of JSON from `gh run list` and `gh api`. I read it with `jq`, or paste it into a spreadsheet. [DuckDB] promises to answer those questions with SQL, straight from the files, without a server to install.

## Who this course is for

You know SQL from [SQL Server], [PostgreSQL] or [SQLite]: `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`. You write C# or Java. You don't need to know anything about analytics or data engineering.

## What DuckDB is, in one table

| | SQL Server / PostgreSQL | SQLite | DuckDB |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runs | as a server | inside your process | inside your process |
| Built for | transactions (OLTP) | transactions, small apps | analytics (OLAP): scans, aggregates, joins over many rows |
| Storage | rows | rows | columns |
| Database | a server instance | one file | one file, or none: it also queries CSV, JSON and Parquet files directly |
| From .NET | `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient`, Npgsql | `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite` | DuckDB.NET (ADO.NET) |
| From Java | JDBC driver | JDBC driver | JDBC driver |

## The data

The course queries a snapshot of this repository's own GitHub Actions history, exported on 2026-09-14 into [`code/duckdb/data`]:

- `runs.json`: 125 workflow runs, from `gh run list --limit 1000 --json databaseId,workflowName,event,status,conclusion,createdAt,updatedAt,startedAt,headBranch,headSha,attempt`;
- `jobs.json`: the 315 jobs of those runs, with their steps, from the GitHub REST API.

They are the runs written by the [GitHub Actions course]: real failures, real timings, three operating systems.

## By the end of this course, I will be able to

- query CSV, JSON and Parquet files with SQL from the DuckDB CLI;
- use DuckDB's SQL extensions to write shorter analytical queries;
- flatten nested JSON with `STRUCT`, `LIST` and `unnest`;
- convert between formats and read many files at once;
- use DuckDB from C# and from Java;
- read a query plan and know when DuckDB is the wrong tool.

## Outline

| # | Lesson | If you know SQL Server |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [First queries] | `sqlcmd`, `OPENROWSET`, `SELECT INTO` |
| 2 | [Friendly SQL: dates, windows, `QUALIFY`, `PIVOT`] | window functions, `PIVOT` |
| 3 | [Nested data: `STRUCT`, `LIST`, `unnest`] | `OPENJSON`, `CROSS APPLY` |
| 4 | [Files: CSV, Parquet, globs, remote files] | `BULK INSERT`, external tables |
| 5 | [DuckDB from C#] | ADO.NET |
| 6 | [DuckDB from Java] | JDBC |
| 7 | [Performance: plans and columnar storage] | execution plans, columnstore indexes |
| 8 | [Persistence, transactions and concurrency] | isolation, locks |
| — | [Journal] | |

## Resources

- [DuckDB documentation]
- [Why DuckDB]
- [DuckDB CLI]
- [Friendly SQL]: the extensions to standard SQL
- [DuckDB source code]

pages.body:
## Progress

- [x] Data snapshot: 125 runs and 315 jobs of this repository
- [x] CI: every lesson's SQL compared with its expected output on three OSes
- [x] Lesson 1: first queries
- [x] Lesson 2: friendly SQL
- [x] Lesson 3: nested data
- [x] Lesson 4: files
- [x] Lesson 5: DuckDB from C#
- [x] Lesson 6: DuckDB from Java
- [x] Lesson 7: performance
- [x] Lesson 8: persistence, transactions and concurrency

## 2026-09-14 — The data

- `runs.json`: `gh run list --limit 1000 --json databaseId,workflowName,event,status,conclusion,createdAt,updatedAt,startedAt,headBranch,headSha,attempt`, exported around 14:04 UTC. 125 runs, the oldest from 2026-09-13 15:53.
- `jobs.json`: one call per run to `repos/spareilleux/learn/actions/runs/{id}/jobs?per_page=100`, keeping 11 fields of each job and 5 of each step. 315 jobs for 121 runs: 4 runs never had a job.
- The jobs endpoint returns the latest attempt only: 4 jobs for the run attempted three times, 12 with `?filter=all`. Noticed while writing lesson 3; the snapshot stays as it is.

## 2026-09-14 — Installing DuckDB

- Locally, `winget` had DuckDB 1.5.3 installed (`DuckDB.cli`), with 1.5.5 available. The course uses 1.5.5, unzipped from the GitHub release.
- CI on Linux and macOS: `curl -fsSL https://install.duckdb.org | sh` → `Successfully installed DuckDB 1.5.5 to /home/runner/.duckdb/cli/1.5.5/duckdb`. The script reads `DUCKDB_VERSION` from the environment, which the workflow sets, so the version is pinned.
- CI on Windows: the script doesn't support it; the workflow downloads `duckdb_cli-windows-amd64.zip` and adds the folder to `GITHUB_PATH`.
- `check.sh` runs each script with `duckdb -csv <` and diffs against `sql/expected/`. Each OS takes one to two seconds for all the scripts of lessons 1-4, the HTTPS query included.

## 2026-09-14 — Surprises while writing lessons 1-4

- `SUMMARIZE`'s `approx_unique` was 131 for 125 unique run ids, and 17 for 21 workflow names.
- The CLI uses the OS time zone for `TIMESTAMPTZ` display (`America/…` locally, UTC on runners): lesson 2's script sets `TimeZone` explicitly.
- `sum(INTERVAL)` doesn't exist, `avg(INTERVAL)` does.
- `labels[0]` returns `NULL` without an error.
- The lambda arrow `x -> …` prints a deprecation warning in 1.5.5; the lessons use `lambda x: …`.
